strengths: Critically addresses an overlooked blind spot in online test-time adaptation (TTA): the implicit assumption of unbounded compute time, which invalidates many empirical conclusions when deployed under real-world latency or budget constraints.

Introduces a rigorous and principled taxonomy of temporal pressure via three archetypes—discrete (environment-driven), continuous (user-driven), and amortised (resource-driven)—each accompanied by interpretable, closed-form utility decompositions (e.g., availability vs. served accuracy, accuracy vs. responsiveness).

Presents a thoughtful critique and refinement of prior evaluation schemes (notably Alfarra et al., 2024), eliminating artificial step penalties, forced pipeline idling, and unrealistic zero-cost fallback assumptions through a buffered single-model pipeline.

Comprehensive empirical study evaluating 7 TTA methods across 15 corruptions and 16 temporal scenarios (240 evaluations), revealing significant rank instability and providing concrete explanations for method failures (e.g., why ETA collapses under strict deadlines while AdaBN or SHOT-IM remain viable).
Exceptionally clear presentation, precise notation, and transparent discussion of limitations and design implications for future deployable TTA methods.
weaknesses: The evaluation is confined to a single backbone architecture (ResNet-50) and a single dataset/shift benchmark (ImageNet-C). Modern TTA methods frequently evaluate on Vision Transformers (ViT) or ConvNeXt, where the balance between forward-pass latency and backpropagation overhead may differ significantly.

All experiments are conducted with a fixed batch size of 64 on desktop hardware (RTX 4080). In many latency-critical edge deployments, inference occurs with small batch sizes (e.g., batch size 1 or 8) on embedded hardware, where gradient-based adaptation overhead profiles could scale differently.

The paper is primarily a diagnostic and benchmarking contribution; it does not propose or validate a novel adaptation method specifically designed to mitigate the identified failure modes (though it clearly outlines design requirements like anytime adaptation and corruption-conditioned compute allocation).

strengths: Critically important and timely motivation: conventional test-time adaptation (TTA) research predominantly optimizes offline accuracy while neglecting the adaptation latency on the critical inference path. This paper formalizes and addresses this discrepancy directly.

Well-formulated evaluation framework: Tempora introduces three well-grounded deployment archetypes (discrete with single-model buffering, continuous with human-perceptual hyperbolic discounting, and amortised resource budgets) with clean mathematical decompositions into availability, responsiveness, and frozen retention.

Compelling and insightful empirical results: Benchmarking seven prominent TTA methods across 16 temporal settings on all 15 ImageNet-C corruptions (240 evaluations) thoroughly demonstrates severe rank instability (ETA loses in over 41% of temporal evaluations) and reveals key failure modes such as computational insolvency.
Clear, structured presentation with high-quality visualizations (e.g., Figures 1–3) and thorough supplementary analysis.
weaknesses: The evaluation is restricted to a single architecture (ResNet-50) and a single high-end desktop GPU (Nvidia RTX 4080). Hardware with different compute/memory profiles (such as edge GPUs like Jetson, CPUs, or mobile NPUs) may show vastly different forward-vs-backward pass ratios and memory bottlenecks.
The paper is strictly evaluative and diagnostic; it does not propose an algorithmic solution or an anytime/time-aware adaptive mechanism that solves the identified failure modes.

In the amortised setting, Tent, ETA, and SAR collapse to near 0.1% accuracy after running for only 7–18 batches before freezing. While interesting, this severe collapse may partly reflect an artifact of specific learning rate / BN update dynamics early in adaptation rather than an insurmountable property of gradient-based TTA, warranting further ablation of early stopping or warmup strategies.

strengths: Important and timely conceptual contribution: While existing test-time adaptation (TTA) benchmarks evaluate models in an unconstrained 'temporal vacuum', real-world deployments are strictly constrained by latency, deadline arrival, or compute budgets. Tempora provides a principled framing of this problem.

Comprehensive and well-grounded framework: The formulation of three distinct deployment archetypes—discrete (environment-led/hard deadlines), continuous (user-led/hyperbolic latency discounting), and amortised (resource-led/budget caps)—meaningfully expands upon the initial time-constrained setting introduced by Alfarra et al. (2024).

Insightful metric decompositions: Each utility metric factors into interpretable components (availability vs. served accuracy; responsiveness vs. accuracy; adapted vs. frozen accuracy), providing clear diagnostic tools for why specific methods fail under temporal pressure.

Pervasive rank instability revealed: The empirical study evaluates seven TTA methods across 16 temporal scenarios on ImageNet-C (240 evaluations), demonstrating clearly that offline rankings (where ETA dominates) fail to predict temporal performance, with gradient-free methods frequently dominating under strict latency.

High clarity and presentation quality: The writing is precise, the visual diagrams (Figures 1, 2, 4) and tables clearly articulate the protocols, and the appendix contains detailed per-corruption logs and protocol justifications.
weaknesses: Limited architectural diversity: The experimental evaluation is conducted exclusively using ResNet-50. Because BatchNorm affine adaptation is central to many studied methods (Tent, ETA, SAR, AdaBN) and behaves fundamentally differently from LayerNorm in Vision Transformers (ViTs), testing only CNNs limits the generalisability of the empirical findings to modern vision architectures.

Restricted to a single hardware setup and fixed batch size (batch size = 64): Wall-clock latencies (both forward and backward passes) vary drastically between desktop GPUs (RTX 4080) and edge compute platforms (e.g., Jetson Orin, Raspberry Pi, mobile accelerators). Furthermore, latency-critical real-time streams often require small batch sizes (e.g., batch size = 1), where backpropagation overhead, batch statistic estimation, and method viability would exhibit substantially different trade-offs.

Unexplored collapse mechanism in amortised evaluation: Gradient-based methods (Tent, ETA, SAR) collapse to 0.1% accuracy during the frozen phase after early budget exhaustion (Table 5 and Table 19). While the authors note this phenomenon, the manuscript does not sufficiently isolate whether this collapse is an optimization pathology of early entropy minimization or an artifact of running statistic tracking in PyTorch BatchNorm layers under small sample counts.

Purely diagnostic contribution without a proposed solution: Tempora identifies three key failure modes and proposes design desiderata (corruption-conditioned compute allocation, time-aware scaling, anytime properties), but does not propose or validate a new TTA method designed to meet these criteria.

strengths: Principled and realistic conceptual framework: Grounding temporal constraints in physical units (ms) rather than model-relative proxies resolves significant methodological issues in prior work (such as Alfarra et al., 2024), including forced idling, stepped penalties from ceiling functions, and unrealistic zero-cost parallel fallback models.

Comprehensive taxonomy of temporal scenarios: Introducing three distinct archetypes—discrete (hard deadlines/sample loss), continuous (interactive/hyperbolic discounting), and amortised (cumulative overhead budget)—provides a multi-dimensional lens covering diverse real-world deployment needs.

Actionable and interpretable utility decompositions: The mathematical decomposition of utility metrics into constituent terms (e.g., availability vs. served accuracy, responsiveness vs. accuracy, and adapted vs. frozen phases) allows researchers to pinpoint exact failure modes (availability collapse, latency discounting erosion, harmful post-freeze adaptation) rather than merely observing rank shifts.

Extensive and rigorous empirical evaluation: The study encompasses 11 TTA methods across over 750 distinct temporal configurations, spanning multiple architectures (ResNet-50, ViT-B/16, ResNet-18), datasets (ImageNet-C, ImageNet-R, ImageNet-V2, CIFAR-10-C), and disparate hardware platforms (Nvidia RTX 4080 vs. Raspberry Pi 5), providing strong empirical backing for the claim of pervasive rank instability.
High clarity and presentation quality: The manuscript is exceptionally well-written, logically organized, and supported by clear visualizations and exhaustive appendices.
weaknesses: Purely evaluative contribution without an algorithmic solution: While the paper identifies three design principles for deployable TTA (input-conditioned compute allocation, time-aware scaling, and anytime performance), it does not propose a concrete method that instantiates these principles or mitigates the observed rank instability.

Simulation vs. live concurrent streaming: The evaluation relies on a discrete-event wall-time simulation driven by profiling measurements rather than an end-to-end live asynchronous testbed, which may abstract away low-level systems effects such as OS scheduling jitter, memory bus contention, and thermal throttling on constrained hardware.

Sensitivity to metric formulation choices: In the continuous utility archetype, the choice of hyperbolic decay and the specific HCI threshold $T$ introduces subjective tuning parameters that strongly modulate the severity of penalty and resulting rank orderings.

strengths: Addresses a fundamental yet overlooked blind spot in online test-time adaptation (TTA): standard evaluations assume unbounded computation time, ignoring the critical latency-accuracy trade-offs inherent to real-time deployments.

Proposes a well-grounded and comprehensive conceptual framework (Tempora) comprising three distinct deployment archetypes: discrete utility (hard deadlines / asynchronous arrivals), continuous utility (hyperbolic decay modeling user responsiveness in interactive systems), and amortised utility (finite compute/energy budgets).

Provides elegant mathematical decompositions for each metric (e.g., availability vs. served accuracy, accuracy vs. responsiveness, adapted vs. frozen performance), which successfully diagnose the underlying failure modes (availability collapse, accuracy erosion, harmful adaptation) rather than merely measuring net performance.

Fixes notable methodological shortcomings of prior work (Alfarra et al., 2024) by replacing model-relative timing proxies with physical units (ms), eliminating unrealistic dual-model fallback assumptions, and mitigating forced idling via a single-slot buffer queue.

Presents an extraordinarily thorough empirical evaluation spanning 11 TTA methods, multiple model architectures (ResNet-50, ViT-B/16, ResNet-18), diverse datasets (ImageNet-C, ImageNet-R, ImageNet-V2, CIFAR-10-C), and distinct hardware environments (RTX 4080 GPU vs. Raspberry Pi 5 CPU).
weaknesses: The evaluation uses offline-measured latencies within a retrospective discrete-event simulation rather than deploying methods in a live, real-time streaming pipeline under operating system scheduling variability and concurrent thread contention.

Experiments predominantly evaluate models with a batch size of 64; many real-world, latency-critical edge deployments operate in sequential single-sample streams (batch size 1), where the ratio between forward pass and backpropagation latency can vary significantly.

All methods are evaluated using their default hyperparameters; while the authors convincingly argue that computational insolvency is driven by intrinsic backpropagation overhead that tuning cannot easily erase, it remains possible that some methods could be adjusted (e.g., adapting every k-th step) to better fit specific temporal regimes.

strengths: Compelling and realistic framing: The paper addresses a major blind spot in current test-time adaptation (TTA) research—namely, that conventional benchmarks evaluate methods in a temporal vacuum assuming unbounded compute time, which fails to reflect latency-sensitive real-world deployments.

Well-motivated taxonomy and utility metrics: Grounding temporal constraints into three operational archetypes (discrete/deadline-driven, continuous/interactive decay, and amortised/resource budget) provides a comprehensive, mathematically clean, and physically grounded evaluation suite.

Diagnostic utility decompositions: Decomposing utility into interpretable factors (availability vs. served accuracy in discrete; accuracy, responsiveness, and covariance in continuous; adapted vs. frozen performance in amortised) effectively uncovers the mechanical root causes of failure (availability collapse, latency discounting erosion, and catastrophic drift upon freezing).

Methodological improvements over prior work: By introducing a single-slot buffer and wall-clock simulation in physical units (ms), the paper resolves key artifacts of prior work (Alfarra et al., 2024), such as forced idling, stepped penalty floors, and reliance on artificial fallback models.

Extensive and rigorous empirical evaluation: The empirical study is comprehensive, evaluating 11 methods across diverse backbones (ResNet-50, ViT-B/16, ResNet-18), datasets (ImageNet-C, ImageNet-R, ImageNet-V2, CIFAR-10-C), and hardware platforms (Nvidia RTX 4080 vs. Raspberry Pi 5 CPU), spanning over 750 temporal evaluation configurations.
weaknesses: No new algorithmic method: The contribution is strictly evaluative and diagnostic. While the paper outlines three necessary properties for deployable TTA (corruption-conditioned compute, time-aware scaling, anytime performance), it does not implement or validate a novel TTA algorithm embodying these principles.

Offline simulation vs. live deployment: The evaluation is conducted via a retrospective discrete-event simulation driven by pre-measured batch execution times rather than an asynchronous multi-threaded system on live streaming physical feeds, which could introduce real-world system noise, pipeline stalls, or memory bandwidth contention not fully captured here.

Sensitivity to metric parameterizations: While parameter ranges are motivated by human-computer interaction (HCI) literature and hardware utilization limits, the utility functions (such as hyperbolic vs. exponential discounting in continuous utility) inherently reflect modeling assumptions that directly influence ordinal method rankings.

Evaluation protocol alignment: Standard default hyperparameters from offline literature are reused throughout. As observed with LAME, evaluating methods designed for specific distribution settings (e.g., non-i.i.d. continuous streams) within an episodic i.i.d. benchmark can disadvantage certain approaches independent of their adaptation overhead.
